definition: This topic surveys the religious texture of Philip K. Dick's fiction across the full run of his novels and short stories, from early satire and alternate-history speculation to the explicitly theological late work.
pkd_relevance: Religion is not an occasional theme in PKD; it is one of the main engines of his fiction. He repeatedly returns to the same problems: how divine truth would appear in a counterfeit world, whether revelation is a voice or a vision, whether Christ is a person, a force, or a pattern of rescue, and how Gnostic, Christian, Buddhist, and Platonic frameworks compete to explain the same uncanny experience.
in_the_fiction: The early fiction already tests religious and apocalyptic structures through unstable worlds and hidden powers. Eye in the Sky turns perception into a theological problem; The Man in the High Castle turns history into a question of providence and hidden order. In the middle period, The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch, Ubik, A Maze of Death, and Faith of Our Fathers bring in false gods, counterfeit sacraments, salvation, and anti-salvation. Later fiction such as Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said and VALIS makes revelation, voices, and second-coming imagery central rather than incidental.
in_the_exegesis: The Exegesis retrofits the fiction into a larger theology. Dick repeatedly treats his novels as encoded attempts to understand Christ, Sophia, the Logos, the Black Iron Prison, and the possibility that the world is both simulated and redeemable. The fiction and the notebooks form a feedback loop: the novels supply images, the Exegesis supplies interpretive systems, and the systems in turn alter how the novels are read.
intellectual_background: The study draws on Christianity, Gnosticism, Judaism, Neoplatonism, Buddhism, Hinduism, and comparative religion. Dick is especially drawn to Pauline resurrection, Johannine Logos theology, apocalyptic expectation, Platonic recollection, and the layered cosmologies of Gnostic and Indian thought.
scholarly_debate: Some critics emphasize Dick's fiction as theology in narrative form, while others stress ideology, paranoia, or philosophical speculation. The best reading probably keeps all of those in view: the novels are religious without being doctrinal, and they use religion to explore reality-testing, power, and the possibility of grace.
chronology_summary: The religious register begins early, deepens through the 1960s, and becomes explicit after 1974. The late novels do not invent religion from nothing; they make visible a pattern that had been developing across the whole fiction.
contradictions_summary: PKD never settles on a single religion. His fiction can portray the divine as saving, deceptive, punitive, gentle, terrifying, immanent, external, or technologically mediated. The tension between liberation and manipulation is part of the point.
editorial_notes: This topic is intentionally synthetic rather than exhaustive. It is a gateway for reading the fiction in religious terms, not a replacement for the work-by-work archive.
open_questions: Is Dick's fiction best read as Christian, Gnostic, or syncretic?
How much of the religious language in the fiction is ironic, and how much is devotional?
Which novels most directly anticipate the Exegesis's theology, and which resist it?
